newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - Amoco's Kazakhstan pact a first.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Amoco's Kazakhstan pact a first.

text.p: Amoco Corp took the first step toward establishing a presence in Kazakhstan by signing an agreement with the Republic of Kazakhstan to join the Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC), T. Don Stacy, president of Amoco Eurasia Petroleum Ltd told Reuters on Wednesday.

"It has long been our goal to establish ourselves there with a significant presence. This is the first step," Stacy said in a telephone interview. "We think the Caspian Sea is one of the greatest unexplored regions on Earth."
Amoco reached an agreement to ship three million tons of oil a year through the CPC pipeline, or about 60,000 barrels of crude oil per day.
Stacy said Amoco's initial investment commitment in Kazakhstan is about $130 million, including $70 million to pay for a 1.75 percent share of pipeline construction costs.
CPC plans to build a 900-mile pipeline from Kazakhstan's Tengiz oil field to an export terminal on the Black Sea.
CPC is reaching the final stages of government approvals. "We think construction will start in probably two to three months, with completion in 1999," Stacy noted.

Initially, Amoco's annual shipment of three million tons of crude will account for about 10 percent of the capacity of the new pipeline. But Stacy noted, "As the pipeline (use) is enlarged, our percentage will go down even though our volume will remain constant."
Amoco also signed an agreement giving it exclusive rights to several exploration and production projects in Kazakhstan.
Burnham Securities analyst Joel Fischer called Amoco's entry into Kazakhstan "a sensible move. It's clear they want to be represented in all major oil provinces of the former Soviet Union."

"If Amoco has earlier production (before completion of the CPC pipeline), we will need to address the transportation issue," Stacy said. "Our agreement with the government of Kazahkstan says they will help us do that."
Separately, Stacy said Amoco is among the bidders seeking rights in Uzen, Kazakhstan's second largest oil field.

"That's an older field, largely developed, though it has fallen on hard times for lack of investment capital," Stacy said. If successful in its bid, Amoco would provide that investment capital and do development on that field, he said.
Besides Amoco's participation, CPC, a $1.5 billion pipeline project, is comprised eight international oil companies and the states of Russia, Kazakhstan and Oman.
Amoco is a global producer of oil, natural gas, refined products and chemicals with revenues of more than $36 billion which ranks it among the top five U.S. producers.
